d14702|The robot is told to "drive straight" but slowly drifts anyway, because the left and right motors and wheels are never exactly the same. The fix is "feedback": use the Gyro to measure which way it is facing, work out the error, and adjust the left and right wheel speeds a little. This experiment uses the simplest method,

61ab28|Slowly raise Kp: the offset gets smaller and smaller. Notice that "heading error at the end" is still a little off: P alone always leaves a small error.
c9a19c|Now make Kp very large (over 9): wobbling appears! This is called "oscillation". The Gyro reading is a little delayed, so correcting too hard overshoots.
cc328b|Raise the "drift" and try again: the bigger the drift, the bigger the error for the same Kp.

1351e4|Think about it: why does the error grow the longer it runs? (Hint: each step's small error adds up.) Some teams use walls, white lines or the Distance Sensor to "re-align" every so often and reset the error to zero.

14927f|The Gyro heading is 0–360°; going past 360° "wraps around" to 0°. If you use "target − current" directly as the error, a target of 350° and a current heading of 10° gives an error of 340° — and the robot turns the wrong way for a whole circle! The right way is to convert the error into the range −180° to +180°:
640caa|Press "350° ← 10°": direct subtraction gives 340°, but the shortest turn is actually 20° to the left.
f7fcd3|Slowly pull the two needles apart: be careful when the direct difference goes over 180°.
